| [THEORY-1208](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1208.md) | Bacterial endosymbionts lose their cell-envelope and envelope-transport genes together below about 400 kb and begin to lose translation genes below about 200 kb, and the host supplies the membranes, transport and protein synthesis that the smallest-genome symbionts no longer encode, as for organelles | The wider thesis McCutcheon, Garber, Spencer & Warren assert, filed beside [THEORY-1049](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1049.md) by the twenty-second status review ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md) §3; [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1). [THEORY-1049](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1049.md), Active, holds what McCutcheon and colleagues' survey shows and what they infer from it; whether the thesis holds is this entry's question, and its promote_when is [THEORY-1049](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1049.md)'s old condition, word for word. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1209](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1209.md) | In genetically identical E. coli, a cell's swarming potential is a transient inherited state: its descendants share it for about four generations and lose it by about seven, and it tracks the cell's iron status rather than a bistable switch | The wide form of Bhattacharyya et al. (2023), [LIT-853](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-853.md), kept here when the status review of 2026-10-30 narrowed [THEORY-179](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-179.md) to what the assays measured and promoted it ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md); [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md), kind 1). The paper asserts a heritable iron memory. Iron was read only through a plasmid promoter reporter, inheritance rests on few founders and four sampled generations, and the delay model is fitted to two time points. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1211](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1211.md) | An endosymbiont becomes an organelle in steps: the host first targets effector proteins into it; an imported host protein redundant with one of its functions then lets the endosymbiont's own gene decay, making it dependent; and a general import pathway, once evolved, brings in hundreds of proteins; this genetic integration arises only in permanent, vertically transmitted associations | The wider thesis Sørensen, Stiller, Kröninger & Nowack assert, filed beside [THEORY-1107](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1107.md) by the twenty-second status review ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md) §3; [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1). [THEORY-1107](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1107.md), Active, holds the scenario Sørensen and colleagues propose; whether the thesis holds is this entry's question, and its promote_when is [THEORY-1107](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1107.md)'s old condition, word for word. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1214](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1214.md) | Cicada hosts whose endosymbiont Hodgkinia has split into many interdependent lineages compensate by sending more Hodgkinia cells to each egg, with Sulcia numbers and the transmission route unchanged, so that every egg still receives every lineage; the raised titre is a host adaptation driven by the symbiont's fragmentation, and a cost of it | The wider thesis Campbell et al. assert, filed beside [THEORY-1106](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1106.md) by the twenty-second status review ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md) §3; [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1). [THEORY-1106](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1106.md), Active, holds what Campbell and colleagues measured and how they read it; whether the thesis holds is this entry's question, and its promote_when is [THEORY-1106](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1106.md)'s old condition, word for word. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1215](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1215.md) | Besides Asgard archaea and the alphaproteobacterial ancestor of mitochondria, Myxococcota and Planctomycetota were major donors of genes to the eukaryotic lineage before its last common ancestor, in waves: Asgard first, then Planctomycetota before the mitochondrion, then the mitochondrial ancestor and Myxococcota together | The wider thesis Bernabeu, Manzano-Morales, Marcet-Houben & Gabaldón assert, filed beside [THEORY-1105](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1105.md) by the twenty-second status review ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md) §3; [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1). [THEORY-1105](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1105.md), Active, holds what Bernabeu and colleagues' reconstruction finds and how the authors read it; whether that is true is this entry's question, and its promote_when is [THEORY-1105](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1105.md)'s old condition, word for word. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1219](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1219.md) | Buchnera's metabolism interlocks with its aphid host's: it makes the essential amino acids its host cannot from host-supplied glutamate and aspartate, depends on the host for the non-essential amino acids and its membrane phospholipids, and cannot live outside the bacteriocyte | The wider thesis Shigenobu, Watanabe, Hattori, Sakaki & Ishikawa assert, filed beside [THEORY-1103](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1103.md) by the twenty-second status review ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md) §3; [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1). [THEORY-1103](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1103.md), Active, holds what Shigenobu and colleagues' genome shows and what they infer from it; whether the thesis holds is this entry's question, and its promote_when is [THEORY-1103](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1103.md)'s old condition, word for word. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1223](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1223.md) | Monocercomonoides exilis lost its mitochondrion only after the organelle's essential functions had been removed in steps, Fe–S cluster assembly to a cytosolic SUF system and then the glycine cleavage system by loss, and the loss required no compensating change elsewhere in the cell | The wider thesis Karnkowska et al. assert, filed beside [THEORY-1098](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1098.md) by the twenty-second status review ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md) §3; [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1). [THEORY-1098](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1098.md), Active, holds what Karnkowska and colleagues' genome analysis finds and infers; whether the thesis holds is this entry's question, and its promote_when is [THEORY-1098](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1098.md)'s old condition, word for word. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1228](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1228.md) | A bacterial endosymbiont becomes genetically integrated, an organelle, when host proteins imported into it replace genes it has lost, and this does not require gene transfer from the endosymbiont: in the Paulinella chromatophore and the nitroplast, the two systems with hundreds of imported proteins, the replacing genes are mostly the host's own or come from other bacteria | The wider thesis Sørensen, Stiller, Kröninger & Nowack assert ("EGT is not a precondition for the genetic integration of an endosymbiont"), filed beside [THEORY-1100](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1100.md) by the twenty-third status review ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md) §3; [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1). [THEORY-1100](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1100.md), Active, holds what the review reports; whether the thesis holds is this entry's question, and its promote_when is [THEORY-1100](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1100.md)'s old condition, word for word. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1265](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1265.md) | Approximating a chemical master equation by a Fokker–Planck or nonlinear Langevin equation gets the quasi-potential right only at the fixed points: between them it mis-estimates the barriers, so escape rates come out wrong by a factor exponential in system size and the approximation can pick the wrong one of two states as the long-run favourite, and its apparent entropy production vanishes at every steady state, missing the dissipation that sustains it | Falasco & Esposito (2025), [LIT-1892](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1892.md), §IV.D–E and §VII.A.1, read in [NOTE-1472](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1472.md); Vellela & Qian (2009), [LIT-1890](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1890.md), appendix A, read in [NOTE-1474](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1474.md). Active: both formulas were checked on the Schlögl model, including Vellela & Qian's counterexample, where the exact and diffusion quasi-potentials favour different states. It does not say diffusion approximations fail near fixed points or for Gaussian fluctuations; there they are exact to leading order. | Active |
| [THEORY-1268](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1268.md) | In a nonequilibrium steady state of a thermodynamically consistent Markov jump network, the entropy produced while a current is counted, times the squared relative uncertainty of that count, is at least 2k_B, independent of the counting time, so a current precise to ε costs at least 2k_BT/ε² of dissipation; the 2015 letter proves this within linear response and for single-cycle networks at any affinity, and for many-cycle networks far from equilibrium shows it numerically and states it as a conjecture | Barato & Seifert (2015), [LIT-1885](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1885.md), read in full in [NOTE-1480](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1480.md). Active for the scope stated in the title: the biased walk, the unicyclic formula (A/N) coth(A/2N) and the bound on random four-state networks were checked numerically. It bounds the precision of currents, not of occupations, so it does not price how long a maintained state lasts, and the general multicyclic proof is not in this paper. | Active |
| [THEORY-1270](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1270.md) | Entropy production does not select which of several maintained steady states is the stable one: in the bistable Schlögl model the state the system occupies in the long run can carry either the higher or the lower deterministic entropy production rate, and the mean stochastic entropy production follows whichever state is more probable; in general the most dissipative attractor is the longest-lived only under special conditions, and lifetime tracks relaxation entropy only near detailed balance | Vellela & Qian (2009), [LIT-1890](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1890.md) (§3.3, Fig. 6), read in [NOTE-1474](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1474.md), show the counterexample; Falasco & Esposito (2025), [LIT-1892](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1892.md) (§§III.F, IV.H, VIII.B.6), read in [NOTE-1472](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1472.md), give the general account: minimum entropy production holds only near detailed balance with linear dynamics, and the two maximum principles hold only where relaxation and escape dissipations nearly coincide. Active as a negative result. It does not refute every extremum principle, only those that rank steady states by dissipation alone. | Active |
| [THEORY-1273](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1273.md) | In a driven chemical system with two stable states and a finite number of molecules, each maintained state is metastable: it is left by fluctuation after a time exponential in system size, set by a barrier in a nonequilibrium quasi-potential that closes at the saddle-node, and the long-run share of time in each state is fixed by the parameters and system size, not by the initial condition; the deterministic rate equation, where the initial condition decides, holds only on times short of that escape time | Vellela & Qian (2009), [LIT-1890](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1890.md), read in [NOTE-1474](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1474.md), on the Schlögl model, with Falasco & Esposito's general frame ([LIT-1892](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1892.md), §§III.C, IV.H, VI; [NOTE-1472](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1472.md)). Active: the slow eigenvalue, the barriers, the initial-condition independence and the closing of the barrier at the fold were checked numerically on the paper's model. It does not say which state is the more stable without computing the quasi-potential, and the paper's own large-volume rate formula carries a spurious 1/V factor. | Active |
| [THEORY-1315](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1315.md) | As a stochastically forced system approaches a fold bifurcation its dominant eigenvalue goes to zero, so it recovers ever more slowly from small perturbations, and under ongoing perturbation this critical slowing down shows as rising lag-1 autocorrelation and rising variance; skewness and flickering are further warnings not caused by slowing; but the same signals, less pronounced, also precede thresholds that are not bifurcations, so they mark proximity to a broad class of thresholds and not which kind, nor when the shift will come | Scheffer et al. (2009), [LIT-1956](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1956.md), read in [NOTE-1536](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1536.md) (Skimmed) from the version reprinted as chapter 2 of Dakos's 2011 thesis. Active for the slowing-down result, which is standard (Wissel 1984), checked in the chapter's Box 2.2 example, and re-derived and simulated here for variance σ²/(2\|λ\|) and autocorrelation e^{λΔ} since the chapter's Box 2.3 was not extractable. The scope and timing caveats are the authors' (p. 31). It does not say the signals have been shown in chaotic systems, which the review calls "less well studied", or that any of the reviewed empirical cases was checked here. | Active |
| [THEORY-1323](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1323.md) | Under weak local noise a many-body operator decays at a rate proportional to its size, so a Hamiltonian's small-sized integrals of motion, which chaotic dynamics does not spread, decay slowly while generic operators, which it spreads, decay fast; in exact diagonalization of Ising and Heisenberg chains of up to nine sites at weak depolarizing noise, the slowest Lindbladian eigenoperators are linear combinations of the known exact and approximate small integrals of motion, and which approximate ones rank among the slowest moves with the noise strength | Yang and Abanin (2025), [LIT-1958](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1958.md), read in [NOTE-1534](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1534.md). Active as a statement of what the paper derived exactly and what its exact diagonalization showed at the sizes it reached. It does not say that the correspondence holds at large system size ([THEORY-1343](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1343.md)), that every integral of motion is found (those above size 3–4 are not), or that slowness ranks conserved quantities independently of the environment. | Active |
| [THEORY-1343](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1343.md) | The first-order picture in which a small integral of motion Q of a many-body Hamiltonian is, under weak local noise, the slowest Lindbladian eigenoperator holds at large system size whenever its leak ε out of span{Q} satisfies ε ≲ γ ≪ 1, because the gap controlling the perturbation is not the exponentially small level spacing but one of order min(γL, √(v_Bγ)), set by the ballistic growth of the operators Q leaks into | Yang and Abanin (2025), [LIT-1958](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1958.md), §IV, read in [NOTE-1534](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1534.md). Proposed because the argument assumes fully chaotic operator growth for the complement, is checked numerically only at nine sites, and is qualified by the authors themselves: hydrodynamic modes give a continuum of slow modes in the Mori limit, so the gap "might not exist at all" outside sectors orthogonal to them. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1368](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1368.md) | Chen, Choi and Mahadevan show that in a quad kirigami sheet read as a linkage the fewest links that rigidify the sheet always outnumber the fewest that connect it, and that under random links the maximum of internal mechanisms, connectivity percolation and rigidity percolation fall at distinct link densities in that order | Chen, Choi & Mahadevan (2020), [LIT-2064](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2064.md), read from arXiv v2 in [NOTE-1574](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1574.md) (main text; the SI with the proofs was not read). Proposed: the minimal counts are proved by construction in the SI, which was not read; the thresholds are numerical, and the rigidity threshold is a peak of a second derivative with a heuristic explanation. Planar quad kirigami and infinitesimal rigidity only; no experiments. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1369](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1369.md) | Chen and colleagues show that marginally rigid origami and kirigami carry a topological polarization, so that a quasi-1D origami strip folds at the edge its pattern angles select and a domain wall between kirigami of different polarizations is flexible though constraints locally match the degrees of freedom, while periodic triangulated origami appears always to have zero polarization | Chen, Liu, Evans, Paulose, Cohen, Vitelli and Santangelo (2016; arXiv 2015), [LIT-2049](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2049.md), read in full in [NOTE-1624](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1624.md). Proposed: the strip result has the authors' own experiment, but the domain-wall result is numerical and the 2D origami claim is a conjecture on numerics. It does not say that joining rigid parts creates freedom in general: equal polarizations give no wall mode, and walls of the other orientation are stressed lines that carry load. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1373](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1373.md) | Combinational logic built from flat-foldable origami switches can be reconfigured by moving the switching elements rather than rewiring them, by rotating the two elements of a gate between series and parallel or by permuting elements among the blocks of a Rubik's-cube arrangement, and so reaches more functions per element than a rewired gate array | Hu, Tan, Chen and Yan (2025), [LIT-2082](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2082.md), read in [NOTE-1608](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1608.md). The rotatable gate, the 30-gate array and a third-order cube switching between full adder and full subtractor were built and tested over all inputs; the densities per cube order and the gate savings are counts against the authors' own baselines. It does not say that the computation is purely mechanical, since outputs and inter-gate signals are electrical, or that the material reconfigures itself. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1374](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1374.md) | Hopkins (2013) holds that a flexure system's freedom space is the intersection of its parallel limbs' freedom spaces and the span of its serial stages' freedom spaces, so the same finite library of freedom–constraint space types suffices to analyse and synthesize any combination of parallel and serial flexures, and comparing constraint orders with the system's constraint space classifies a design as exactly, over- or under-constrained | Hopkins (2013), [LIT-2069](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2069.md), read in full in [NOTE-1580](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1580.md). Proposed: the rules follow from linear reciprocity of screw spaces and are stated with design examples, but there is no experiment and no independent check, and the library's completeness rests on Hopkins (2010), [LIT-2042](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2042.md). It excludes interconnected limbs, is kinematic only, and its over-constraint test says nothing of misfit stress. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1377](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1377.md) | Li and Choi show that the rigidity of general origami patterns can be tuned by enforcing or relaxing the planarity of selected facets, and that the critical density at which a pattern reaches its minimum number of degrees of freedom depends on the facet-selection rule, the number of candidates sampled per step and the fraction of triangular facets | Li & Choi (2026), [LIT-2068](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2068.md), read in [NOTE-1564](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1564.md) (main text; the Supplementary Notes were not read). Proposed: one group's simulations on ten patterns. The n − 3 count is proved; the dependence of the critical density on rule, pool size and triangular-facet ratio is numerical, and the formula for it is fitted, not derived. Rigidity is infinitesimal at one folded configuration, and the "critical density" is a fixed-size statistic, not a thermodynamic threshold. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1386](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1386.md) | A neural network trained only on the equilibrium and energy conditions of a truss model of conical Kresling origami recovers its energy curve and inverts it to geometries with prescribed stable heights and barrier, and stacks of such cells with ascending barriers fold in the designed order under compression | Kang, Kim, Yang and Ryu (2025), [LIT-2086](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2086.md), read in [NOTE-1619](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1619.md). Forward and inverse results are checked against a beam-truss FEA that shares the network's truss abstraction; the folding order is checked also in one scaled PET prototype, where barriers differ from prediction and are compared after normalizing to the bottom layer. It does not say the truss model captures the mechanics of real cells. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1389](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1389.md) | Connelly and Whiteley prove that for tensegrity frameworks first-order rigidity implies prestress stability, which implies second-order rigidity, which implies rigidity, that none of these implications reverses even for bar frameworks, and that whether a first-order flex extends to second order is decided by a Farkas-type test on the framework's proper self-stresses | Connelly and Whiteley (1996), [LIT-2080](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2080.md), read in part in [NOTE-1588](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1588.md) (§§1–3, 4.4, 5.1–5.2 and 6 in full; the proof of Theorem 4.3.1 and the later examples skipped). Proposed: the hierarchy and the stress test are stated in the abstract and the sections read, but the main proof was not read. It is about local rigidity, not global rigidity, and it does not say that every first-order flex of a non-rigid framework extends to a finite motion. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1390](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1390.md) | Hopkins (2010) holds that all freedom–constraint space pairs of a flexure-guided rigid body fall into 50 types, that only those whose constraint space holds enough pure-force lines can be realised by parallel flexures while the rest need modules stacked in series, and that where linear actuators must act to drive the permitted motions without parasitic error is set by the flexures' stiffness and not by the freedom space alone | Hopkins (2010), [LIT-2042](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2042.md), read in part in [NOTE-1596](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1596.md) (chs. 1, 2.1–2.2, 4.1–4.4, 4.7 and 5; the type catalogue, ch. 3, and the stiffness-matrix derivation, §§4.5–4.6, were not read). Proposed: the 50-type count rests on a catalogue and appendix not read, the thesis is not peer reviewed, and the actuation result has one experiment behind it, which located the least-error actuator line near the prediction while measuring errors much larger than predicted. It is quasi-static and small-motion, and says nothing about actuating serial systems. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1398](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1398.md) | In mesoscopic simulation, DNA origami folds hierarchically: accessible structures collapse into a locally ordered precursor that then crystallizes, while larger structures with interior geometry are often caught in global topological traps that early progress does not predict | DeLuca, Duke, Ye, Poirier, Ke, Castro and Arya (2024), [LIT-2081](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2081.md), read in [NOTE-1561](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1561.md). A simulation result, ten runs per design, in a model without misbinding, helical topology, base stacking or annealing. It does not say that real origami traps this way, nor that the precursor is a nucleus: the paper does not use the word for its mechanism. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1399](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1399.md) | Silverberg and colleagues show that the square-twist origami, whose crease pattern admits no rigid folding motion, folds by bending its facets, and that the ratio of bending to crease stiffness, together with the plane angle, sets a critical transition between monostable and bistable folding | Silverberg et al. (2015), [LIT-2100](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2100.md), read in [NOTE-1554](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1554.md) (the letter in full; SI pp. 1–2 skimmed). Proposed: one group's experiments on paper and gel with matching simulations, on a single unit cell. The general thesis that the number of degrees of freedom changes with the energy scale probed is the authors' framing; what was shown is this one structure. Tessellations are proposed, not tested. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1400](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1400.md) | An array of non-volatile bistable origami switches laid out one module per minterm can be programmed to any combinational function of its inputs by a mobile actuator that sets the modules it passes, so programmability moves from rewiring into an addressing path that origami logic itself steers | Chen, Tan and Yan (2025), [LIT-2030](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2030.md), read in [NOTE-1559](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1559.md). Built and tested for 2- to 4-input arrays (half and full adder and subtractor, 2-bit adder or multiplier); generality to any function is by construction over pre-built minterm modules. It does not say that the device programs itself: the address path is fixed by a magnet layout designed outside it, and the robot runs on electric motors. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1403](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1403.md) | Deng and colleagues show that a soft composite whose magnetic particles are held in a meltable polymer can have its magnetization pattern rewritten by local laser melting under a programming field and fixed again on cooling, so one film can be given many different shape responses to the same actuation field | Deng, Sattari, Xie, Liao, Yan and Lin (2020), [LIT-2034](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2034.md), read in [NOTE-1565](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1565.md), as a neighbour of Yeow, Yang and Ren (2024), [LIT-2113](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2113.md). Proposed: the figures were read by caption, and the supplement on cycling only by its caption. It does not say that the film can be rewritten in place without an external laser and field, nor anything about an actuator coupling to and decoupling from a separate structure. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1405](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1405.md) | Kinoshita and Ohsaki show that a bistable compliant truss mechanism, whose second stable state comes from snap-through stopped by contact with an obstacle, can be converted into a single-piece frame mechanism with the same function by optimizing thin pseudo-joints at its former pin joints under a strain cap, without lumping deformation into a point hinge | Kinoshita and Ohsaki (2009), [LIT-2029](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2029.md), read in full in [NOTE-1597](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1597.md). Proposed: the conversion is shown on one seven-node example, in simulation, with equivalence judged by overlaid force–displacement curves. It does not say that the frame is bistable without the obstacle, that the method finds frames without a truss to start from, or that a fabricated frame behaves as computed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1406](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1406.md) | Hopkins (2007) holds that for a rigid stage held in parallel by ideal wire-like flexures under small motions, the motions the stage permits and the lines along which a constraint can be added without changing them determine each other uniquely as reciprocal screw spaces, and that for pure-force constraints these pairs fall into 26 types indexed by the number of non-redundant constraints | Hopkins (2007), [LIT-2031](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2031.md), read in part in [NOTE-1592](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1592.md) (the argument chapters; the case-by-case derivation of the types, chs. 7–8, was not read). Proposed: the reciprocity is standard screw theory and the one-to-one link is shown in §5.3, but the count of 26 rests on an enumeration not read here, and the thesis is not peer reviewed. The count holds only for ideal pure-force constraints; the thesis itself finds more types once wrenches of any pitch are allowed. It says nothing about stiffness, dynamics or actuation. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1408](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1408.md) | Kane and Lubensky show that in isostatic lattices the number of zero modes in a region equals a local count of sites and bonds plus a topological count fixed by winding numbers of the bulk equilibrium matrix, so that gapped phases of different topological polarization carry protected floppy modes or states of self-stress at their boundaries and interfaces even where degrees of freedom and constraints locally balance | Kane and Lubensky (2014; arXiv 2013), [LIT-2078](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2078.md), read in full in [NOTE-1601](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1601.md), the supplementary proof included. Proposed: the theorem is proved and the two models agree with it; an independent case is what promotion asks. Chen et al. ([LIT-2049](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2049.md)), read in this batch, apply the topological polarization to an origami strip and to kirigami and are a candidate. It does not say that every boundary mode is topological, or that the linear zero modes extend to finite motions. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1411](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1411.md) | Stern, Arinze, Perez, Palmer and Murugan show in simulation that a creased thin sheet trained by repeatedly folding it under example force patterns, with each crease softening when a supervisor judges the fold correct and stiffening otherwise, comes to fold unseen test force patterns into the correct class's structure, because the heterogeneous stiffness it acquires eliminates most folded structures and enlarges the basins of a few | Stern, Arinze, Perez, Palmer and Murugan (2020; arXiv 2019), [LIT-2116](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2116.md), read in [NOTE-1615](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1615.md) from the arXiv v1 preprint, titled differently; the PNAS text and the Supplementary Notes were not read. Proposed for that reason. It is a result about a model: it does not say that any physical sheet has been trained, that the sheet learns without an external supervisor, or that it scales beyond small two-class tasks. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1414](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1414.md) | Rocks and Mehta show that stating Maxwell–Calladine counting in terms of elastic susceptibilities gives an index theorem that holds with prestress and heterogeneous stiffness, in which the zero-displacement tensions are the states of self-stress while the forces that excite each linear zero mode follow the joint symmetry of geometry and energy, so that prestress breaking a geometric symmetry redirects and localizes those forces without changing the mechanisms | Rocks and Mehta (2024; arXiv 2022), [LIT-2112](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2112.md), read in [NOTE-1557](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1557.md) (the main text; the appendices with the proofs skipped). Proposed: the theorems' proofs were not read, and the symmetry-breaking result is shown on two small symmetric examples. It is a linear theory: it does not say when prestress makes a structure rigid, which the authors leave to a nonlinear analysis, nor whether zero modes extend to finite motions. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1415](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1415.md) | A series stack of decoupled bistable Kresling barrels is a Preisach memory whose reachable states are fixed by the order of the switching thresholds, while hidden elastic degrees of freedom admit defect states that the loading protocol cannot reach and can leave only irreversibly | Jules, Reid, Daniels, Mungan and Lechenault (2022), [LIT-2072](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2072.md), read in [NOTE-1617](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1617.md). Shown in experiment on one four-barrel stack and its softer twin, with the Preisach graph confirmed and defect states found by twisting by hand. It does not say that the 64 counted states were all observed (39 of 48 single-defect states were), that the readout identifies every state, or that loading alone can create a defect in a decoupled stack. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1417](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1417.md) | Zang, Zhao, Misseroni and Paulino show that prestressing Kresling origami cells with controllable springs tunes each cell's energy barrier and stability continuously, so that reordering the barriers of cells in an assembly makes folding sequences feasible that the unprestressed assembly cannot follow | Zang, Zhao, Misseroni & Paulino (2025), [LIT-2091](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2091.md), read in [NOTE-1569](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1569.md) (the main text; the SI was not read). Proposed: one group's model and prototypes, with three-cell assemblies and a theory that misses the panel buckling seen in experiment. The "frustration" is prestress applied from outside, stored elastic energy, not an incompatibility inside the crease pattern. Of 56 ordered transitions in the three-cell stack, prestress opens the 8 blocked by the ordering of the barriers; the 16 that need intermediate states stay unachievable. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1418](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1418.md) | Stern, Pinson and Murugan show that a crease pattern designed with one folding motion still has exponentially many distractor branches meeting at the flat state, created by frustrated loops of two-branch vertices, so folding it reliably needs actuators placed so that the regions they can each fold correctly cover the sheet | Stern, Pinson & Murugan (2017), [LIT-2074](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2074.md), read from the arXiv v1 preprint in [NOTE-1571](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1571.md); the published version and the SI were not read. Proposed: simulations on idealized rigid-panel vertices with zero-temperature descent, actuation statistics from one 4 × 4 pattern, and folding islands offered as a heuristic, not a necessary and sufficient condition. The authors limit the difficulty to the flat state. The analogy to SAT and protein folding carries no hardness proof. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1419](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1419.md) | Damavandi, Hagh, Santangelo and Manning show that, for elastic energies quadratic in their constraints, constraint counting predicts energetic rigidity only when the system has no states of self-stress, and that when it has them the spectrum of the prestress matrix decides whether second-order rigidity implies energetic rigidity, with no general result when that matrix has negative eigenvalues | Damavandi, Hagh, Santangelo and Manning (2022; arXiv 2021), [LIT-2041](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2041.md), read in full in [NOTE-1570](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1570.md). Proposed: a single paper's derivations, with the hardest case left open by the authors. It does not say that a system with states of self-stress is never energetically rigid, nor that the shear modulus measures rigidity; and it covers Hookean energies only. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1420](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1420.md) | The sublevelset persistent homology of an energy landscape contains its disconnectivity graph as the zero-dimensional part and also records alternative transition paths and higher critical points, and for the alkane torsional landscape it has a closed form in every dimension | Mirth, Zhai, Bush, Alvarado, Jordan, Heim, Krishnamoorthy, Pflaum, Clark, Zhang and Adams (2021), [LIT-2047](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2047.md), read in [NOTE-1616](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1616.md), appendices with the full proofs skimmed. The first two parts are standard correspondences the paper states and illustrates; the closed form is its Theorems 1 and 2. It treats one scalar energy only: nothing here covers several resources at once, which would need multi-parameter persistence. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1423](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1423.md) | Berry, Lee-Trimble and Santangelo show that near the flat state a non-intersecting rigid origami vertex with positive Gaussian curvature has a configuration space split into two components (popped up and popped down) that no rigid, non-tearing motion joins, while a negative-curvature vertex's components stay joined by a neck | Berry, Lee-Trimble and Santangelo (2020), [LIT-2024](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2024.md), read in full in [NOTE-1605](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1605.md) (arXiv v1). Proposed: the single-vertex result follows from the second-order condition hᵀQh = K, whose proof to quadratic order the authors call somewhat involved, and is confirmed numerically on one symmetric 5-fold vertex. It does not say anything far from the flat state or at large curvature, it does not hold when faces may pass through each other, and its multi-vertex extension is conditional. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1425](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1425.md) | Rocks and colleagues show that in disordered spring networks a chosen linear strain response between a distant pair of target nodes and a pair of source nodes, and several such responses at once, can be produced with near-total success by removing about one percent of the bonds, chosen greedily with an analytic update built from the network's states of self-stress and compatible stress | Rocks, Pashine, Bischofberger, Goodrich, Liu and Nagel (2017; arXiv 2016), [LIT-2060](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2060.md), read in [NOTE-1607](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1607.md) from the arXiv v1 preprint; the PNAS text was not reached. Proposed for that reason and because the Supporting Information was not read. It is a linear, athermal result for central-force networks made rigid first: it does not say why the chosen bonds work, that the network could find them itself, or that allostery in proteins works this way. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1427](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1427.md) | Chen and Santangelo show that a flat triangulated rigid origami sits at a singular point of its configuration space where generically 2^Vi folding branches meet, one pair for each pattern of vertex popping states, so folding from flat is exponentially ambiguous | Chen and Santangelo (2018), [LIT-2021](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2021.md), read in [NOTE-1614](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1614.md) (main text in full, appendices skimmed). Proposed: the count of 2^Vi branches is numerical for Vi from 2 to 8 and proven only for H1 triangulations, which are rare; second-order solutions are treated as configurations without a general guarantee; and only patterns with four boundary vertices are treated. It does not say how the branches join away from the flat state, or that a real sheet misfolds at any measured rate. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1428](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1428.md) | Evans, Silverberg and Santangelo show that a lattice theory of origami tessellations predicts that the soft deformations of a Miura-ori sheet are edge modes decaying from its boundaries with an analytic decay length, so that its number of degrees of freedom scales with its perimeter, not its area | Evans, Silverberg & Santangelo (2015), [LIT-2070](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2070.md), read in part in [NOTE-1587](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1587.md) from arXiv v2 (the derivations were skimmed). Proposed: a linear theory about one ground state with facet bending coarse-grained as folds, checked on one 8 × 8 paper sheet, with the decay length for a pop-through defect estimated only to within 100%. Registered as a stand-in for Silverberg et al. (2014); it does not carry that paper's claims of bistable cells or crystal-like defects. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1431](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1431.md) | A multistable origami metamaterial driven by a fixed sequence of tension and compression can serve as the reservoir of a reservoir computer: a trained linear readout of its sequence of stable configurations classifies inputs better than the same readout of the raw inputs, and a retained buffer of cells carries input history | Liu, Fang, Xu and Wang (2023), [LIT-2026](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2026.md), read in [NOTE-1600](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1600.md). The comparison with the raw inputs (90.4% against 87.2% on binarized MNIST) and the memory result are simulations with a least-action model; the experiment covers ten 5×4-pixel digits on a 4×2-cell prototype. It does not say that the material learns: only the linear readout is trained. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1433](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1433.md) | Krishnakumar and Suresh show that compliant mechanisms can be designed by topology optimization without pseudo-densities, by removing material where the topological derivative of a mutual-to-weighted-input-and-output strain-energy objective is lowest, which yields designs without point hinges and lets one parameter trade geometric against mechanical advantage | Krishnakumar and Suresh (2015), [LIT-2099](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2099.md), read in full in [NOTE-1582](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1582.md) from a lab-posted manuscript, as a stand-in for Sigmund (1997). Proposed: hinge-freedom is shown by pictures of a handful of coarse-mesh designs, and the η trade-off on one example. It is the authors' account of their own method, not of Sigmund's; it does not say that the designs stay hinge-free under stress constraints or large deformation, or that they were built. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1437](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1437.md) | Cumberworth and Reinhardt review simulation results indicating that, in DNA origami, a staple's later domains bind without a second translational entropy penalty once its first domain is bound, while each loop closed with the scaffold adds a penalty that depends on the order of binding, so that in the small designs simulated staples tend to bind fully once started and assembly needs no nucleation barrier, unlike DNA bricks | Cumberworth and Reinhardt (2025), [LIT-2121](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2121.md), read in part in [NOTE-1626](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1626.md) from the submitted version. The account is the review's synthesis of coarse-grained simulations, mostly the authors' own, of small 2D designs; the authors note evidence that staples do not bind fully once started in larger 3D lattice designs, and the experimental evidence on origami hysteresis they report is mixed. The models sections were not read. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1438](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1438.md) | Marras, Zhou, Su and Castro show that DNA origami joints made of stiff double-stranded bundles connected only by single-stranded scaffold restrict thermal motion to one designed degree of freedom whose range and stiffness are set by connection length, that a crank–slider and a Bennett linkage assembled from such joints follow their rigid-body motion paths, and that the Bennett linkage, rarely found unaided in its higher-energy compacted state, is held there by added bridging strands and released by toehold-mediated strand displacement, each move taking about a minute | Marras, Zhou, Su and Castro (2015), [LIT-2118](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2118.md), read in [NOTE-1635](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1635.md) (main text and figure captions; the Supporting Information unread). Proposed: the conformational statistics are negative-stain TEM fractions on a surface, which the authors call upper bounds, over 52 to 918 particles with misfolds excluded, and one actuation cycle is reported. It does not say that the mechanisms fold with high yield, that switching survives repeated cycles, or that the grid fractions are those in solution. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1439](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1439.md) | Dunn and colleagues show that a DNA origami template with several approximately degenerate well-folded shapes can be annealed to different distributions of those shapes by changing only which staples stabilize intermediates: weakening the cooperative long-range seam staples shifts the products strongly toward the fold that short-range staples favour, and strengthening short-range staples suppresses the fold in which one of them must bridge long range, while in their kinetic model strong early seam contacts trap about half of folding runs | Dunn, Dannenberg, Ouldridge, Kwiatkowska, Turberfield and Bath (2015), [LIT-2135](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2135.md), read in [NOTE-1643](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1643.md). The shift is shown by AFM shape counts on one tile, one anneal ramp and one buffer, with 36-62% of candidate objects fitted; the trapping figure (52% misfolds with full seams, 1% with broken ones) is the model's. The equal stability of the final folds is the authors' design argument, not a measurement, and the model is not thermodynamically self-consistent. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1440](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1440.md) | Sobczak reports, from work in the Dietz group, that 3D DNA origami folds cooperatively within a structure-specific window of about 5 °C and can be folded at a constant temperature within it, while melting occurs 5–10 °C higher and within seconds against minutes to hours for folding, so that on laboratory timescales there are temperatures at which a folded object persists but does not form | Sobczak (2018), [LIT-2138](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2138.md), read in part in [NOTE-1644](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1644.md), standing in for Sobczak, Martin, Gerling and Dietz (2012), [LIT-2131](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2131.md), whose abstract says the same in kind. Measured by gel and SYBR Green assays, mostly on one brick family. The last clause is an inference from the hysteresis: no experiment held a melted object inside the band and watched it stay unfolded, and no melting temperature for the brick was found in the text read. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1441](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1441.md) | Schneider, Möritz and Dietz show that, in isothermal folding at 50 °C of one multilayer DNA origami brick, staple domains bind in a defined order set more by the scaffold's topology of connectivity than by their binding strength, the two termini of a staple bind independently, and a set of early-binding nucleating domains forms a compacted intermediate without which the object still folds but hours later by a slower pathway | Schneider, Möritz and Dietz (2019), [LIT-2122](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2122.md), read in [NOTE-1641](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1641.md). One object, one temperature and one buffer; progress normalized per reaction, so the delay is in when signals saturate, not in a measured yield; the single-terminus kinetics come from a model that assumes the independence it reports. It does not say that topology alone sets the order: the authors' Results call local sequence and connectivity "two important factors". | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1442](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1442.md) | Lee Tin Wah and colleagues show, from AFM snapshots of Rothemund's tall rectangle adsorbed out of solution along a slow cooling ramp, that with 52 nM of each staple folding nucleates at the top and bottom ends between about 65 and 55 °C and grows toward the centre, and that raising the central staples to 670 nM while lowering the outermost edge-row staples to 1.2 nM makes folding nucleate at the centre instead, which they attribute to the concentration dependence of staple melting temperatures under thermodynamic rather than kinetic control | Lee Tin Wah, David, Rudiuk, Baigl and Estévez-Torres (2016), [LIT-2137](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2137.md), read in [NOTE-1625](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1625.md) (main text and supplement). Proposed: one design, one lab, the two concentration changes made together with a slower ramp. The title asserts where folding starts under each allocation and the authors' attribution; it does not assert that the final object or its yield is unchanged, that a fixed stock was reallocated, or that the mechanism is established. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1443](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1443.md) | Wagenbauer, Wachauf and Dietz show that multilayer DNA origami with up to 7% of its staples omitted looks the same as the complete object under negative-stain TEM averaging and agarose-gel mobility, while a gel-based fluorescent de Bruijn probe for unpaired bases tells them apart and estimates that complete reactions still leave 44 to 263 of 7,560 bases unpaired, 96.5% to over 99% quality, depending on design and folding schedule | Wagenbauer, Wachauf and Dietz (2014), [LIT-2128](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2128.md), read in [NOTE-1637](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1637.md). The indistinguishability under TEM and gel mobility is shown directly; the residual counts are extrapolations from a calibration that assumes each omitted staple adds exactly its own bases unpaired, with a background floor near the best result. It does not say how defects are spread across particles, nor anything about misfolds that leave bases paired. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1444](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1444.md) | Douglas and colleagues report that custom multilayer DNA origami on a honeycomb lattice folds in one pot, at 7 to 44 % of scaffold in monomer, only with week-long thermal ramps at about 16 mM MgCl2 and low NaCl, short ramps, low Mg2+ or high Na+ giving slow-migrating, grossly misshapen products, whereas flat and six-helix-bundle origami fold in 72-minute ramps | Douglas, Dietz, Liedl, Högberg, Graf and Shih (2009), [LIT-2130](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2130.md), read in [NOTE-1629](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1629.md) (main text and captions; the Supplementary Information unread). Proposed: per-target yields and the six-helix-bundle data are in the unread supplement, yield is a gel-band fraction and quality is judged by eye. The title asserts the reported conditions and outcomes; it does not assert the authors' conjecture that multilayer structures traverse harder kinetic traps, nor any mechanism for the cation effects. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1445](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1445.md) | Aksel, Navarro, Fong and Douglas report that choosing DNA origami staple breakpoints by a shortest-path search over a weighted graph, scored by an equilibrium free energy summing staple binding, scaffold loop closure and hybridization at 50 °C, raised the gel-measured yield of accurately folded multilayer blocks from 2-6% to 48-61% in four published designs, three of them with unchanged scaffold route and helix layout, with yields correlating with the model's score | Aksel, Navarro, Fong and Douglas (2024), [LIT-2125](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2125.md), read in [NOTE-1642](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1642.md). The yields are integrated gel intensity in a hand-bounded window after one 21 h anneal, with no stated replicates and TEM only of the redesigns; the correlation is R² = 0.86 over 8 designs from the same four structures. The largest gain (10×10, 2 to 61%) also changed the scaffold seam and paired fraction. The score is equilibrium and ignores folding kinetics and inter-staple cooperativity, so the account is one of more stable parts, not of a chosen pathway. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1446](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1446.md) | Majikes and colleagues find, across 34 designs of one 2D DNA origami rectangle annealed under deliberately poor conditions and scored by AFM classification, that defectivity tracks design-level aggregates: the skew of the distribution of loop-entropy penalties each fold would pay if it bound first and the measured melt temperature are its principal correlates, a linear combination of these with a staple-blocking metric collapses it onto one trend, and designs with more short folds at the expense of medium folds are more defective | Majikes, Hasni, Haridas, Robertson, Pintar, Zwolak and Liddle (2026), [LIT-2127](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2127.md), read in [NOTE-1639](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1639.md). Defectivity is a class-weighted AFM proxy for missing or blocked staples, useful for comparison only; the combination is fitted on 28 designs of one shape, with linear models, and a LASSO over more metrics swaps the blocking term for positive inter-domain cooperativity. The poor-anneal conditions are argued, in supplementary sections not read here, to preserve the ordering seen under standard anneals. The authors' reading that 2D origami assembly is funnel-like rather than path-like is their interpretation of the fit. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1447](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1447.md) | Dannenberg and colleagues show, in a thermodynamically self-consistent domain-level kinetic model of planar DNA origami, that cooperativity between staples from scaffold loop closure and coaxial stacking sharpens the folding transition and produces folding/melting hysteresis, and that the hysteresis is asymmetric, faster cooling or fewer staples lowering the annealing temperature far more than they raise or move the melting temperature, because binding rates are nearly temperature-independent while unbinding rates rise steeply with temperature | Dannenberg, Dunn, Bath, Kwiatkowska, Turberfield and Ouldridge (2015), [LIT-2129](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2129.md), read in [NOTE-1645](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1645.md). A simulation of one 166-domain tile, with parameters chosen to match the scale of hysteresis in one SYBR Green experiment. It does not say that origami has alternative stable states or kinetic traps: the model has a unique equilibrium at each temperature and no misbinding, and its hysteresis shrinks with slower ramps. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1448](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1448.md) | Ni and colleagues show that, in DNA origami cross-tile self-replication, binding a monomer tile to a template raises the effective concentration of its tethered sticky ends from about 1 nM to about 0.8 mM and shifts their melting temperature by about 50 °C, that a two-state model with three entropy terms, fitted once, predicts the melting temperatures of 1- to 4-tile assemblies to about 2 °C, and that with externally supplied tiles, a thermal cycle and UV crosslinking the per-cycle replication rate falls from about 1.9 for dimers to 1.6 for tetramers | Ni, Zhou, Zhu, Bershadsky, Ai, Wang, Sha, Seeman and Chaikin (2026), [LIT-2124](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2124.md), read in [NOTE-1630](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1630.md). The effective-concentration figure is the model's estimate, with a FRET fit of about 0.2 mM; the 2 °C agreement is over assemblies up to tetramers; the replication rates are one figure whose definition is in a supplementary figure not read. The paper's predicted upper limit on string melting temperature, and with it the feasibility of replicating very large patterns, is extrapolation; in experiment tetramers barely separated before the tiles unravelled. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1449](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1449.md) | Zhou, Sha, Ni, Seeman and Chaikin show that, in a non-enzymatic DNA origami dimer replicator fed fresh monomers each thermal and UV cycle, a species arising only by a designed mutation of about 3.5% per copy reaches parity within five cycles and dominates after about nine when its growth rate per cycle is higher, growth rate being the only fitness the system has, while two species that grow alike approach equal shares | Zhou, Sha, Ni, Seeman and Chaikin (2021), [LIT-2126](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2126.md), read in [NOTE-1628](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1628.md), as the stand-in for He et al. (2017), [LIT-2132](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2132.md), whose replicator it extends. The 3.5% is computed from a 16% per-monomer mismatch rate measured by AFM counts; the takeover is one run of 13 cycles counted by AFM, with the fit's equations and per-cycle rates in an SI not read. Fitness here is assigned by the recognition-strand design, and monomers, temperatures and UV are supplied every cycle, so it says nothing of a population that maintains its own conditions. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1450](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1450.md) | Douglas, Bachelet and Church built a DNA-origami barrel whose opening is governed by two aptamer locks forming a logical AND gate over cell-surface antigen inputs, so that the device stays closed and reconfigures to expose its payload only when both designated keys are present, with the key concentration needed to open set by the lock-duplex length, activation at about 10 pM for 16 to 23 bp against about 1 nM for 30 to 44 bp | Douglas, Bachelet and Church (2012), [LIT-2136](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2136.md), read in [NOTE-1634](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1634.md) (main text and captions; the Supporting Online Material, with the lock-length data, unread). Proposed: one lab, a proof of principle, conformations read by TEM counts and flow cytometry. The title asserts the gate and the lock-length dependence; it does not assert that the device can revise its rule, which it cannot, nor anything about cycling, holding costs or clinical use. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1451](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1451.md) | Winfree and Bekbolatov show, in kinetic Tile Assembly Model simulation and kinetic-trap theory, that replacing each tile of a tile set with a K×K block whose internal bonds are unique keeps the logical assembly unchanged but forces any mismatch to stall until it dissociates, raising the optimal speed for a target error ε from r ≈ βε² to r ≈ βε at K = 2; their thermodynamic argument predicts an error rate exponential in K, and the simulated gain beyond K = 2 falls short of it, which they attribute to facet-roughening errors that proofreading does not correct | Winfree and Bekbolatov (2004), [LIT-2119](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2119.md), read in [NOTE-1640](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1640.md) from the authors' submitted preprint. Simulation and kinetic-trap theory, with trap rates fitted and no rigorous proof. It does not say that proofreading has been shown in DNA, that its gain is exponential in practice, or that it corrects every error: growth on facets, nucleation of boundaries and implementation errors are outside it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1452](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1452.md) | Scheckenbach, Schubert, Forthmann, Glembockyte and Tinnefeld show that folded DNA origami can be repaired from strands supplied in solution, transiently bound labels regenerating indiscriminately after photobleaching and staples being taken up selectively where damage or design exposes a scaffold toehold, so that a matching staple pool keeps 76 % of nanorulers intact over 11 days in 0.2 % serum against 12 % without; such self-healing fails to outpace damage at higher nuclease levels, and damage to the scaffold cannot be repaired | Scheckenbach, Schubert, Forthmann, Glembockyte and Tinnefeld (2021), [LIT-2139](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2139.md), read in [NOTE-1636](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1636.md) from the main text; the Supporting Information, which holds the toehold experiments and the 10% serum data, was not read. It does not say that origami repairs itself without supply, that nuclease damage is shown to expose toeholds, or that repair restores every damaged structure: missing staples were replaced in about half. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1453](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1453.md) | Cumberworth, Frenkel and Reinhardt show, in Monte Carlo free-energy calculations of a domain-level lattice model of small planar DNA origami, that typical designs with two-domain staples and edge or single-domain staples assemble downhill with no nucleation barrier, that a maximum-crossover design with three-domain staples has a barrier of about 10 kBT, about 20 kBT at domain resolution, at its melting temperature which vanishes a few degrees below it, and that the presence and height of the barrier are set mainly by coaxial stacking between adjacent staples, not by hybridization strength | Cumberworth, Frenkel and Reinhardt (2022), [LIT-2134](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2134.md), read in [NOTE-1638](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1638.md). Equilibrium simulation of four designs of at most 27 domains with averaged energies. It does not say that a barrier changes folding times or yields, which are not simulated, nor that it causes the hysteresis seen in temperature ramps, which the authors explain but do not reproduce, nor that larger designs have no other barriers. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1454](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1454.md) | Majikes and colleagues find, in a single-fold DNA origami model measured by FRET melting with affine baseline correction, that closing a fold with an already anchored staple is unimolecular and more stable than bimolecular binding of the same domain, and that the fold's melting temperature falls as fold distance grows, by more than 10 °C from short to long, through a configurational-entropy cost; from this they infer, without testing it, that origami folds by nucleation and growth, a staple's longest domain binding first and short, entropically cheap folds then making neighbouring folds cheaper | Majikes, Patrone, Schiffels, Zwolak, Kearsley, Forry and Liddle (2020), [LIT-2117](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2117.md), read in [NOTE-1632](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1632.md) (main text, captions and tables; the supplement unread). Proposed: one fold and one melt domain, measured on the melt only, with equilibrium assumed and not tested. The title asserts the measurement and that the authors infer the pathway; it does not assert the pathway, which the authors say needs systems with multiple folds, nor anything about hysteresis, kinetics or whole-origami yield. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1455](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1455.md) | Shirt-Ediss, Torelli and colleagues report that, for four DNA origami designs each folded from three scaffold sequences with fully complementary staples under one protocol, the sequence that their energy model scored highest in off-target staple–scaffold, scaffold–scaffold, staple–staple and hairpin binding gave the fewest well-folded AFM objects in every design (0–20% against up to about 66–75%), and they attribute the loss to kinetic trapping and scaffold aggregation | Shirt-Ediss, Torelli, Navarro, Khamis, Kaplan, Trewby, Elezgaray, Moradzadeh, Haydell, Keppner, Famulok, Armstrong and Krasnogor (2026), [LIT-2123](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2123.md), read in [NOTE-1627](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1627.md). The ordering of best against worst is shown for four shapes with one off-target-prone exemplar each, replicated in a second lab for two; the de Bruijn control did not always win. Trapping is the authors' hypothesis: aggregation is seen, no trap is located, and GC content and synthesis route are not controlled. The wording of the title is the reader's. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1456](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1456.md) | Rothemund shows that a 7-kilobase single-stranded scaffold routed through a shape, with about 200 unpurified staple strands in excess designed to bind only the scaffold, folds in one two-hour anneal from 95 °C to 20 °C into designed shapes about 100 nm across, with AFM-judged yields of well-formed structures from about 1% to 90% by design and at least 70% for rigid designs on circular scaffold; he proposes, without testing, that strand invasion, staple excess and cooperative staple binding account for this | Rothemund (2006), [LIT-2120](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2120.md), read in [NOTE-1631](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1631.md). The folding is demonstrated; the yields are judged fractions of AFM fields with small counts that mix folding with deposition and tip damage; the mechanism is the author's argument. It does not say that the folded shape is the equilibrium state, nor anything about folding temperature, kinetics or hysteresis, which were not measured. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1457](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1457.md) | Majikes, Patrone, Kearsley, Zwolak and Liddle find, in a single-fold DNA origami model with a topology-reporting fluorophore and quencher, that the folded-state yield after annealing rises with staple excess to a turnover between about 1x and 5x and then falls, below 50 % at high excess for fold distances of 131, 1187 and 3407 bases, independent of staple motif and unchanged by a twofold slower anneal, as an equilibrium model predicts when each fold domain can be occupied by a separate staple, the blocked state, with folded over blocked equal to the fold's j-factor over the free staple concentration; they propose, without testing it, that whole origami escapes this through cooperativity and strand displacement along a nucleation front | Majikes, Patrone, Kearsley, Zwolak and Liddle (2021), [LIT-2133](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2133.md), read in [NOTE-1633](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1633.md) (main text, captions and tables; the supplement, with the slower-anneal control, unread). Proposed: one lab, one fold at a time, one reporter channel that cannot tell blocked from unbound, and one fold distance declared anomalous by assumption. The title asserts the single-fold measurement and that the authors propose the whole-origami escape; it does not assert the escape, nor that the blocked state is a kinetic trap. | Proposed |
